title: Priors as scientific statements
dek: A prior p(θ) is part of the model. “Flat” is not empty. The scale you put the flatness on is the scientific choice.
story: Write p(θ) the way you write f(y|θ): in public. A Uniform(0,1) on a probability is a statement. A Uniform on logit(π) is a very different statement, concentrating mass near π = 0 and 1. Calling either “noninformative” is advertising, not mathematics.

Weakly informative priors in a genomics lab encode scale: a log-odds coefficient is probably not 20; a district SD is probably not 50 on the logit. They regularise separation and keep MCMC in the interior. They should still lose to the likelihood when n is large.

Prior predictive checks: draw θ from p(θ), then y from f(y|θ), and ask whether the implied MIC ranges, case counts, or allele frequencies look like the world you work in. If the prior predictive lives on another planet, the posterior started there too.
deep: Improper priors (p(θ) ∝ 1 on ℝ) can yield proper posteriors in nice GLMs and fail in mixed models (variance components). A sampler that “sort of ran” is not a proof of propriety. Prefer a proper weakly informative prior on scales.

Hierarchical priors are how you stop pretending 40 mutation-specific error rates are unrelated: θⱼ ~ N(μ, τ²), with priors on μ, τ. That is a scientific claim of exchangeability, not a computational trick. If one gene is a known outlier mechanism, it should not share that θⱼ distribution blindly.
Jacobian warning: a prior that is flat on σ is not flat on log σ. Always name the parameterisation. The same goes for π versus logit π versus the two Beta parameters.
Sensitivity: for rare events, show two or three priors you could defend in lab meeting. If conclusions flip, the data were not decisive — that is the result.

example.title: Flat on logit is not flat on π
example.setup: A colleague puts N(0, 10²) on β₀ in an intercept-only logit, calling it “weak.” Translate to π.

steps.title: Push forward
steps.body: β₀ ~ N(0,100) implies π = logit⁻¹(β₀) is almost a point mass at 0 and 1 with a thin bridge. Most prior draws are π ≈ 0 or 1 — a strong claim about a resistance probability.

steps.title: A lab-scale alternative
steps.body: N(0, 1.5²) on the log-odds scale puts most prior mass between about 0.05 and 0.95 on π. Still wide. Still named.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Simulate prior predictives of y in n = 20. If half the fake studies are 0/20 or 20/20 while your disease is not like that, the prior is not “weak” in the world you study.

example.takeaway: Name the scale. Simulate y. Then defend p(θ) as you would defend a likelihood.

check.prompt: A prior that is uniform on logit(π):
choices: Is uniform on π as well
Puts heavy mass near π = 0 and π = 1 after the inverse-logit transform
check.answer: Puts heavy mass near π = 0 and π = 1 after the inverse-logit transform
check.why: The Jacobian of the logit map piles mass at the ends of (0,1). Uniformity is parameterisation-dependent.

whyWrong.Is uniform on π as well: Only a uniform on π does that.
whyWrong.Is the unique noninformative prior: There is no unique empty prior.

check.prompt: Beta(2,8) has mean a/(a+b) equal to:

whyWrong.0.25: 2/8, missing the sum in the denominator.

check.prompt: On the prior plate, why is the U-shaped curve labelled as a claim about extremes?
check.figureHint: Three Betas including a wide U-shape.
choices: Because Beta(0.5,0.5)-like shapes put extra prior mass near 0 and 1
Because that curve is a likelihood
check.answer: Because Beta(0.5,0.5)-like shapes put extra prior mass near 0 and 1
check.why: Jeffreys for Bernoulli is Beta(½,½). It is a statement that extremes are more plausible a priori than 0.5 — often the opposite of a lab intuition for a rare allele.

whyWrong.Because U-shaped priors are uniform: Uniform is Beta(1,1), the first curve.
whyWrong.Because Fisher information is U-shaped: I(π)=1/(π(1−π)) is U-shaped, which is why Jeffreys is; the plate is still a prior drawing.
